title: Megatsunami
description: Very large wave created by a large, sudden displacement of material into a body of water
wiki_lead:
A megatsunami is an extremely large wave created by a substantial and sudden displacement of material into a body of water.
Megatsunamis have different features from ordinary tsunamis. Ordinary tsunamis are caused by underwater tectonic activity (movement of the earth's plates) and therefore occur along plate boundaries and as a result of earthquakes and the subsequent rise or fall in the sea floor that displaces a volume of water. Ordinary tsunamis exhibit shallow waves in the deep waters of the open ocean that increase dramatically in height upon approaching land to a maximum run-up height of around 30 metres (100 ft) in the cases of the most powerful earthquakes. By contrast, megatsunamis occur when a large amount of material suddenly falls into water or anywhere near water (such as via a landslide, meteor impact, or volcanic eruption). They can have extremely large initial wave heights in the hundreds of metres, far beyond the height of any ordinary tsunami. These giant wave heights occur because the water is "splashed" upwards and outwards by the displacement.
Examples of modern megatsunamis include the one associated with the 1883 eruption of Krakatoa (volcanic eruption), the 1958 Lituya Bay earthquake and megatsunami (a landslide which resulted in wave runup reaching 524.6 metres (1,721 ft)), the 1963 Vajont Dam landslide (caused by human activity destabilizing sides of valley), and the 10 August 2025 Tracy Arm landslide and tsunami, which reached a height of 481 metres (1,578 ft). Prehistoric examples include the Storegga Slide (landslide), and the Chicxulub, Chesapeake Bay, and Eltanin meteor impacts.

Overview

A megatsunami is a tsunami with an initial wave amplitude (height) measured in many tens or hundreds of metres. The term "megatsunami" has been defined by media and has no precise definition, although it is commonly taken to refer to tsunamis over 100 metres (328 ft) high. A megatsunami is a separate class of event from an ordinary tsunami and is caused by different physical mechanisms.
Normal tsunamis result from displacement of the sea floor due to movements in the Earth's crust (plate tectonics). Powerful earthquakes may cause the sea floor to displace vertically on the order of tens of metres, which in turn displaces the water column above and leads to the formation of a tsunami. Ordinary tsunamis have a small wave height offshore and generally pass unnoticed at sea, forming only a slight swell on the order of 30 centimetres (12 in) above the normal sea surface. In deep water it is possible that a tsunami could pass beneath a ship without the crew of the vessel noticing. As it approaches land, the wave height of an ordinary tsunami increases dramatically as the sea floor slopes upward and the base of the wave pushes the water column above it upwards. Ordinary tsunamis, even those associated with the most powerful strike-slip earthquakes, typically do not reach heights in excess of 30 m (100 ft).

grok_lead: A megatsunami is a tsunami characterized by an exceptionally large runup height of at least 35 meters, often reaching hundreds of meters in confined bodies of water, and is primarily triggered by massive subaerial or submarine landslides rather than typical seismic activity. Unlike conventional tsunamis, which rarely exceed 30 meters in runup and propagate across ocean basins, megatsunamis produce highly localized waves with devastating energy confined to coastal fjords, reservoirs, or narrow inlets, resulting from sudden and enormous displacements of sediment or rock into water. These events are rare, occurring on geological timescales, and their study relies on historical records, geological evidence, and numerical modeling to assess hazards. The primary causes of megatsunamis include large-scale landslides, such as rock avalanches or debris flows, which account for approximately 80% of documented cases, often destabilized by earthquakes, heavy rainfall, or glacial melting exacerbated by climate change. Other triggers encompass volcanic flank collapses, as seen in explosive eruptions, or hypothetical asteroid impacts, though the latter remain unconfirmed in modern records. For instance, incremental collapses of oceanic island slopes, like those proposed for the Canary Islands' Cumbre Vieja volcano, have been hypothesized to generate transoceanic waves, but recent modeling indicates such events produce only modest far-field impacts of 1-2 meters due to gradual material failure rather than instantaneous slides. Seismic tsunamis, while common, seldom qualify as megatsunamis unless they initiate secondary landslides. Notable historical examples illustrate the destructive potential of megatsunamis. The 1958 Lituya Bay event in Alaska, triggered by a magnitude 7.8 earthquake-induced rockslide of 30.6 million cubic meters, produced the highest recorded runup of 524 meters, stripping vegetation up to that elevation and killing five people, though confined to the bay's narrow geography. Similarly, the 1963 Vajont Reservoir disaster in Italy involved a 270-million-cubic-meter landslide into the dammed lake, generating a 250-meter overtopping wave that devastated downstream villages, causing nearly 2,000 deaths despite the dam structure remaining intact. More recently, a 2023 rockslide in Greenland's Dickson Fjord, linked to glacier retreat from climate warming, unleashed a 200-meter tsunami that oscillated as a seiche for nine days, producing global seismic signals and underscoring emerging risks in polar regions. Scientific catalogs, such as the Global Historical Megatsunamis Catalog (GHMCat), document 40 verified events since 1674, predominantly in landslide-prone areas like Alaska, Norway, and Indonesia, with runups ranging from 35 to 525 meters. These records highlight that while megatsunamis pose severe local threatsâeroding coastlines, inundating infrastructure, and altering ecosystemsâtheir far-field propagation is limited, reducing widespread oceanic risk compared to standard tsunamis. Ongoing research emphasizes improved monitoring of unstable slopes and climate-driven instabilities to mitigate future occurrences.
